newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan insurance talks close without deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan insurance talks close without deal.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese trade negotiators ended two days of talks Saturday on opening Japan's insurance market with Washington and Tokyo still far apart on key issues, senior U.S. trade negotiator Ira Shapiro said.

"The distance between our positions on the key issues remains significant," Shapiro told reporters in San Francisco at the close of the talks. "After a period of time in which we saw some modest progress, there has been, I think, an absence of progress, and on some issues, a clear absence of progress."
Shapiro said the United States would continue to pursue a resolution to the dispute.
"We are determined to make every effort, and continue making every effort, to reach a successful resolution of this matter by the Dec. 15 deadline," Shapiro said.

He said the United States hopes to reach a comprehensive agreement before the end of the year. "If there are actions taken after that time, in the absence of an agreement, then we'll respond appropriately at that point," he said.

At issue is Japan's $382 billion domestic insurance market. Washington is pressing Japan to liberalize its primary insurance markets before a niche area called the "Third Sector," where U.S. firms have been dominant, is opened up to Japanese insurers.
The Third Sector includes areas such as personal accident, illness and nursing care, and stand-alone cancer policies.
The dispute has become a major trade irritant between the two countries. They had originally set a July 31 deadline to settle the dispute, but recently agreed to push back the deadline to Dec. 15.

"From the U.S. standpoint, we remain committed to the same objective that we have pursued throughout this negotiation -- the proper implementation of the 1994 insurance agreement between the United States and Japan," Shapiro said.

"And what that means, from our standpoint, is clear. It means significant primary sector deregulation, which benefits not only foreign providers and insurers, but benefits Japanese consumers," Shapiro said.
